title: Symptom checker apps and urgency advice: a narrative review of accuracy for a regional listing decision
abstract: This review summarises what is known about how accurately symptom checker apps assign urgency levels, distinguishing studies that use clinician-written vignettes from studies with real users, and sets out what a health authority should ask of companies seeking endorsement. Findings will be reported after screening.
introduction: Health authorities are asked to endorse digital triage tools for their patient websites. Most evidence comes from vignettes written by clinicians, which may overstate accuracy, and the apps change every few months.
methods: The authority librarian searches three bibliographic databases and two grey literature sources. One reviewer screens and extracts, with the librarian checking a random fifth of screening decisions. Studies are classified as clinician-written vignette, lay-worded vignette or real-user studies, and results are tabulated by class and app version without pooling.
results: Screening has not started. The report will present each evidence class in its own table, with under-triage of emergencies and over-triage of self-care cases alongside overall accuracy.
discussion: The discussion will focus on the gap between vignette and real-user evidence and on version drift. It will end with the questions the committee should put to the two companies.
limitations: Single reviewer; rapidly changing apps; little real-user evidence.
conclusion: To be written after screening. It will not recommend listing on vignette evidence alone.
summary: Narrative review draft structured for SANRA.
